p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for just over six months, and AR 2207 is open at criticality 1 before the readiness board, with the second test article's life test starting this summer.
In Washington he told the partners the truth: the ship will cost about $2.6 billion, eight percent over budget, and a formal notice is due by July 30.
He also declared the last fourteen days of the window, February 18 to March 4, as a schedule reserve that's reported every month.
He told Ada the money was short, straight, and she said she'd always seen his budget face, eyes up and to the left as if there were a spreadsheet on the ceiling, and her count is 774.
On the day of the review he forgot his late wife Grace's birthday, July 14, until Ada's log reminded him.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Frances Odum. Chair of Families of Ares.
Arlo Dunn. The stand's night technician, thirty one, from Limon.
Ada Okafor. Sam's daughter on Ares Station.

Saturday, July 16, 2061. 7:10 AM. The clay pot was where it had always been, on the back step to the left of the door, where it got the morning sun and the afternoon shade off the garage. Sam had flown home from National on Friday night and slept nine hours, which he hadn't done since February, and come out in his socks with his coffee to keep a promise.

Grass, mostly. Gone to seed, the heads bent over the rim. A runner of bindweed that had come up through the drainage hole and around the outside and back in over the top, as if it wanted to see what was in there. The soil had pulled away from the sides in a dry ring you could put a finger down. The glaze on the rim had a crack he didn't remember, and then did: the winter of 2049, the night it went to fourteen below, and Grace out here in his parka with a hair dryer on an extension cord, because she'd said a pot is a living thing too, and he'd said it really isn't, and she'd been right about the crack.
He knelt and parted the grass with two fingers, and found the stick.

A wooden plant marker, the flat kind, gone silver from twelve summers. She'd written on all of them in black marker that was supposed to be permanent, and it nearly had been. He could read N N E T S. The rest had weathered off into the grain. BONNETS, it had said. He'd watched her write it at the kitchen table with her tongue between her teeth, the spring before she got sick.

He didn't pull it out. He held the tablet over the pot and recorded thirty seconds: the grass, the bindweed, the stick, his own thumb at the edge of the frame. One way light time nine minutes and forty three seconds. Grass, he said. Like I said. And this. I'm leaving it where it is. Then he filled the kitchen pitcher and watered the pot, because the spigot on the back of the house had leaked since spring and he'd never fixed it, and he went inside and wrote HOSE WASHER on the list on the refrigerator, under page five.

July went the way Washington had left it. The money was in the partners' hands until their August meeting. The ARA's financial office had the program's paperwork, whatever it said. And the building had split down the middle without anybody deciding it should.

Sam noticed it first at lunch. The software people ate at the north end of the cafeteria, by the windows, and the hardware people at the south end, by the trays, and the long table in the middle where the integration crew had always sat, mixed, was half empty by the second week of July. Rafa's sprint demos had started getting two propulsion engineers instead of six. Hana's stand reports had started going to Rafa's team as attachments with no message in the body. Quinn said it was the budget. Wendell said it was the summer. Rafa said, It's the valve, Sam. Everybody's tired of being careful around it.
On Monday, July 25, a packet came in from Ares Station that wasn't an answer to anything.

ARES STATION ENGINEERING PACKET TO HALCYON BREATHER INTEGRATION FROM C. OKONKWO, BREATHER OPERATIONS. Proposal. The Breather's control code should run on our bench before it runs on our plant. We have the old plant's spare controller and a stack simulator Teodor built from scrap. Our sensors are ours: they drift the way Mars makes them drift. Your simulator's sensors are polite. We can give you one four hour bench window a sol, starting the week of August 8. The spare controller is also our only spare. If we break it, we have no spare. Five of us want in. We'll be the ones running this plant for twenty years. Understood as: we'd like to be on the team, not on the distribution list. Three questions back to you. Who decides when a test stops? Who decides what counts as a pass? And who do we argue with?
Sam read it twice at his desk, and then a third time standing up, because of the last line. Quinn came and read it over his shoulder and put both hands flat on the desk.
That's seventeen people, she said. On two planets. On one bench that's also their only spare.
Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 573.
Every crew fights in the simulator. Mine did that winter, and I was sure I knew how to make them stop.

112 days before launch. oh six hundred, sim 14. full crew, full loop, full departure. oh seven fifteen, Tate humming on the loop. stopped when Mori came on. oh seven twenty, abort call argument, round four. Mori wants the call in the pilot seat. Tate wants it on the engineer's panel, where the data is. oh seven thirty one, Tate: you'll call it late because you want to fly it. Mori: you'll call it early because you're scared of it. loop quiet 9 seconds. oh seven thirty two, Lise: copy all. next step. good commander. oh nine hundred, debrief. Mori and Tate not speaking. to each other. to me, fine. eleven hundred, moved Tate aft in the sim and to the other end of the crew table. Mori forward. fixed. fourteen hundred, wrote the abort call into the flight rules as commander's call. didn't ask them. quicker. sixteen hundred, Wendell: does the crew know about cycle 3. told him the crew has enough to think about. seventeen thirty, L minus 112. quiet loop all afternoon. I called it peace.

Tuesday, August 2. The first bench run on Ares Station was eight days out, and Rafa had a plan for it on the whiteboard in the big room. It was a good plan for a test on Earth. A test conductor at Watkins would call each step on a voice loop, the station would execute it on the bench and call back the result, and Watkins would call the next step. Forty one steps. Rafa had already booked the simulator bay for the loop.

Quinn had the light time on her tablet. Ten minutes and thirty seven seconds this morning, one way, and climbing a little every day. Some time on the afternoon of Tuesday the ninth it would pass eleven minutes. After that, the shortest possible time between a question and its answer would be twenty two minutes, before anybody on either end had thought about it at all.

Twenty two minutes a step, she said. Forty one steps. That's fifteen hours of loop. Their window on the bench is four. And it keeps going up. Next summer, at the worst, it's just over twenty one each way. This cycle it never quite gets to twenty two one way. It only gets there both ways, and it gets there next Tuesday.
Rafa looked at the board for a while. Every instinct I've got says a test needs a conductor.

The three questions from Chiamaka Okonkwo, who ran Breather operations on the station, were still pinned beside the whiteboard. Who decides when a test stops? Who decides what counts as a pass? And who do we argue with?

Quinn, Rafa, and Chiamaka write it over three packets. Every procedure goes up a sol ahead. Every step carries its own rule: if this reading, continue and log it; if that one, stop and safe the bench; if anything else, stop, safe, and ask. The station's test lead owns every stop, because nobody on Earth can make one in time. Watkins owns the morning review, and every answer it sends starts with the step number and the words understood as. The procedure goes up on Thursday. The packet that comes back has a line at the bottom from Chiamaka. First time Earth has trusted us with a stop. Thank you. Three questions attached.

When the delay is physics, design the work around it: send everything ahead, write the hold criteria into the procedure, and give the decision to the people who'll be there when it has to be made. Then close the loop with a review and read backs. That's a communication strategy with a feedback loop, and it's empowering the team.

Thursday, August 4. Rafa had set up a channel in the team's chat tool on Monday, named it BREATHER JOINT, and added everybody. By Thursday morning it had three hundred and twelve messages in it. The station engineers, whose messages went up and down on the relay with everyone else's, had answered the same question about the stack simulator's pressure range three times, to three different people, and one of the answers had been wrong and corrected and the correction had been asked about twice.
Paloma had written from Albuquerque at 6 AM. I've read every message in BREATHER JOINT and I don't know what we decided. Is that a me problem?

Quinn drew it on the whiteboard. Twelve dots, the joint team before Mars: ten at Watkins, two in Albuquerque. Lines between every pair. Then five more dots, off to the right, with a wavy line between them and the rest that she labeled 11 MIN. Then she stopped drawing lines, because there were too many.
Garrett had stopped by the doorway on his way somewhere. Easy. Everything to and from Mars goes through Sam. One voice. Nobody gets crossed.

Quinn writes it on one page and the team argues with it for an afternoon, which improves it. The decision log is where decisions live; if it isn't in the log, it wasn't decided. Each topic gets a pair, one at Watkins and one at the far end: stack simulator, sensor drift, fault logic, procedures, and Paloma's chamber data. Questions for the station go in the morning packet with the pair's names on them, and BREATHER JOINT stays open for chatter, with a pinned note at the top. Paloma replies within the hour. Okay. Not a me problem.

Seventeen people have 136 possible channels. The answer isn't to shut them, or to put one person in the middle of all of them. Design which channel carries what: one record for decisions, named owners for each topic, and a structured path for anything that crosses the delay.

Monday, August 8. Two days before the first bench run. Quinn had written five words on the big room whiteboard on Friday and nobody had erased them: FORMING, STORMING, NORMING, PERFORMING, ADJOURNING. Under STORMING she'd drawn a small arrow and written the word us.

It was fair. The station engineers had started to say, politely, that they felt like Earth's test equipment. Rafa's engineers had started to say, less politely, that they felt second guessed by people who'd never seen the code. One of the station's packets had come back with a line that wasn't a question: Last month Earth changed a procedure overnight and we found out on shift. The hold rules said who could stop a test. They didn't say who the team was.

Garrett's office had sent down a template from HR on Friday. TALLGRASS TEAM CHARTER, VERSION 3. Fourteen pages, a values page with EXCELLENCE, INTEGRITY, VELOCITY in large type, and a box on page one for the team name.
The program's charter said what Sam could decide. It didn't say anything about how seventeen people on two planets were supposed to disagree.
Chiamaka's packet that morning had one question, not three. Before we run anything Wednesday, can we agree how we argue?

It takes three packets and two very long mornings. Quinn holds the pen, which is a log, and both ends write in it. On Wednesday morning it's one page.BREATHER JOINT TEAM AGREEMENT REV 1 AUGUST 10 2061. WHY WE EXIST: TO HAND ARES STATION A BREATHER ITS OWN ENGINEERS TRUST, BECAUSE THEY'LL RUN IT FOR TWENTY YEARS. WHO DECIDES: THE STATION TEST LEAD OWNS EVERY STOP ON THE BENCH. WATKINS OWNS THE CODE. PASS AND FAIL ARE WRITTEN BEFORE THE RUN, BY BOTH. NO PROCEDURE CHANGES INSIDE 24 HOURS OF A RUN WITHOUT THE STATION TEST LEAD'S YES. EVERY ANSWER STARTS WITH THE QUESTION NUMBER AND "UNDERSTOOD AS." QUESTIONS IN THE MORNING PACKET ARE ANSWERED IN ONE SOL. DISAGREEMENTS GO IN THE LOG WITH A NAME, AND THE TWO PEOPLE TALK THE SAME DAY. NOBODY ARGUES ON THE LOOP. NO MESSAGES TO THE STATION 2200 TO 0600 STATION TIME UNLESS SOMEONE COULD GET HURT. REVIEWED EVERY FIFTH RUN.Seventeen names under it. That afternoon the station runs all forty one steps inside one window and holds once, at step twenty nine, by the rule. At the Monday meeting Sam says one thing about it. We're storming. It's a stage. This is how we get through it.

Establish expectations at the team level with the team: why it exists, who decides what, and specific rules for how it works, written by the people who'll keep them, at both ends. Then say when you'll review it. Naming the stage out loud helps people see storming as normal.

Friday, August 12. Wendell turned seventy at the stand. Arlo had driven a cake in from a bakery in Limon, a white sheet cake with blue piping, and somebody had found two candles, a 7 and a 0, and stuck them in crooked. Wendell looked at it for a long time with the thermos lid on his knee and said he'd been asked four times that day when he was quitting, and it was his birthday, and could they not.
The life test on the second test article was in its fourth week. Cycle 1,140 at lunch, clean so far, which Wendell said meant nothing yet. Wendell had been on or near the console for most of them.

Quinn had the resource histogram on her laptop. Wendell's line ran at a hundred and eighteen percent from August into October. His name was on four activities on the critical path between now and the Cape: the valve work, the stage's acceptance firing, the shipping test, and the propellant loading rehearsal at the Cape in the summer of 2062. At the end of the schedule were the fourteen days of declared reserve. None of them would help if the person on four critical activities wasn't there to do them.
Garrett had an idea, which he'd sent that morning with a cake emoji. Knowledge capture sprint. Two weeks, Wendell writes it all down. Then we're covered.

Quinn rebuilds the propulsion resource plan that afternoon, with Wendell on the phone and a slice of cake on her keyboard. Wendell goes to eighty percent, no more than four nights in seven. Arlo goes on the plan beside him on every stand activity, by name. Hana's deputy goes beside him for the acceptance firing. Tuesday afternoons are paid and booked: Wendell, Arlo, Quinn, a recorder, and one question each week. The first one is Quinn's. What do you listen for first? Wendell thinks about it. Ask me what it sounds like. Don't ask me to write it. She doesn't. Arlo writes it, in the spiral notebook.

A person who's the only one who can do critical work is a resource constraint. Plan the resource as it really is: realistic hours, a trained backup on each critical activity, and the knowledge transfer built into the plan as work, not added on top.

Tuesday, August 16. The integration loop was a weekly call, an hour on Tuesdays, and since the station joined, the recording went up in the next morning's packet, so the five engineers on Mars could hear Earth argue a day late.

The item was the first autonomy build. Rafa's team needed a model of the main oxidizer valve that behaved the way the real one did, including the bad cycle, so the build could be tested against it. The only measured data on the bad cycle was AR 2207's: 2059 and the April campaign. The report had been open since February. Hana had said, twice, in writing, that the raw traces would go to software when the root cause team signed them off, and not before. In May somebody had proposed a filter that would have hidden exactly that event, and she hadn't forgotten it.
That morning Rafa had said, on the loop, with seventeen people and a recorder listening: Propulsion has been sitting on that valve's data since 2059. We all know how that went.
Hana had said nothing. She'd left the call. By noon she was sending everything for software through Quinn, and Rafa was sending everything for propulsion through Quinn.
The joint agreement was taped to the wall above the standup board. NOBODY ARGUES ON THE LOOP. It had been in force for six days.

Rafa first, in his office. He knows. He says it before Sam can. It was a cheap shot. My team thinks the build's going to slip and it'll be on us. Then Hana, at the stand, on the upper deck behind the oxidizer tank. It takes her a while. He said it where everyone could hear it. Including Mars. And then the real thing: she's afraid the model will be used to tune the rebound away, the way the filter would have. Together, Wednesday, with Quinn and the whiteboard. Rafa needs the valve's real behavior, bad cycles included. Hana needs a promise that nothing built on it will ever hide the event. What they write: the raw traces go to software under a rule that the model must reproduce the rebound, never suppress it, and any fault logic that uses it gets a propulsion review. Hana's engineer sits in Rafa's sprint reviews. On the next Tuesday loop, before the first item, Rafa apologizes, on the recording, to the same seventeen people. Hana says, Accepted. The station's packet the next morning has one extra line. We heard. Thank you for letting us hear that too.

Find the source before you pick a mode: here, fear on both sides about the same data. Talk to each person privately first, then together, and collaborate on what each actually needs. Treat the remark as a ground rule violation and repair it where it happened.

Saturday, August 20. Wendell had left his thermos in the blockhouse after the cake, and he didn't own another one, so Sam drove it out to Byers on Saturday morning and handed it to him over a screen door. Wendell said thanks and closed the door, which was a whole visit with Wendell.

On the way back, in Strasburg, Sam pulled off I-70 for the hose washer that had been on the refrigerator list since July. Kiowa Creek Hardware was a long low building with a feed store at one end and a key machine at the counter by the register. A woman was cutting a key on it with her back to the door. Straight graying blond hair. A navy fleece. When she turned around with the key in her hand, it was Bea Kowal.
She didn't drop the key. She looked at him the way you'd look at weather you'd seen coming.

Washers are aisle four, she said. Then, after a while, I resigned in June. My sister's place is six miles south. They needed somebody who could do keys. She rang up a man buying chicken feed. When he'd gone, she said, You read my files.

She told him at the counter, between customers, in her square, careful voice. Friday, September 19, 2059, 7:30 AM, a conference room on the second floor. Garrett, Hana, the program's chief engineer, her, and the agency's deputy director on the phone. Wendell had a third repro attempt on the stand schedule for Monday the 22nd, and the stand was also needed that week for the qualification firing the September 30 review wanted to see. Everybody wanted September clean. So did I. The agency asked whether the date would move if it stayed open. Hana walked us through the stand data, and her hands were shaking. Nobody said close it. Somebody said can we, and nobody said no. She put the key on the counter. It took twenty two minutes. I timed it later, off the calendar. They cancelled the third attempt in the room. Work order 59-3318. I was the one with the pen.
A woman came in for a padlock. Bea sold it to her. Then she put both hands on the counter, the way Quinn did.
Don't make me testify, Sam. I can't sit at that table. I can say it to you in a hardware store. That's all I've got.

He doesn't say anything for a while, because she needs him not to. Then he tells her what he can promise. I won't be the one who makes you. I can't promise the board won't ever ask. I don't get to promise that. And what he has to do. Work order 59-3318 is in our own files. On Monday the board gets it from me, with nobody's name on it. That part isn't yours to carry. She nods as if he'd passed something. He asks whether she'd write the rest down, in her words, for the anomaly record, and send it herself or through him, her choice. She says she'll think. He buys the washer. On Monday the work order goes to the board's clerk, pulled from the company's own records. The next Saturday an envelope comes to the house in Aurora, square capitals on the outside. Four pages, headed STATEMENT OF B. KOWAL FOR THE ANOMALY RECORD OF AR 2207, with the date, the room, and the twenty two minutes. Clipped to it is a note. Send it where it goes. If they need me after that, they can ask me. Not you. B. He sends it to the clerk the Monday after, as her statement, with her note on top.
Monday, August 29. 5:40 AM. The two note chime. He'd stopped thinking of Mars as close.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3742. One way, 11 minutes 57 seconds. Margin, 729 days. Hi, Dad. I'm going to be angry in this one. I've never done that in a log, so you'll have to tell me how it comes out. Good news first, because Mom always did good news first and then the dentist. Four of the six came up. In Bay D, by the air handler. Pilar named them, and I'm not telling you the names, because you'll laugh, and then I'll have to explain them, and it's late. I saw the stick in your video. I know what it says. It says N N E T S now. Leave it there. July's been sitting in my pocket like a rock. I mean that nicely. Okay. Angry. On Thursday the ARA held a briefing for the families in Denver. Somebody's sister streamed it into the queue and half the station watched it at breakfast. The agency said, on the agency's model, Halcyon gets here with fifty eight days to spare. They had a chart. It had a green band on it. And then the families did what families do, they sent messages. Pilar's mother sent her a cake recipe, Dad, a cake recipe, because the margin was so comfortable. Teodor's brother told him to stop worrying. Two people on my shift stopped turning their bunk lights off at nine at night. Nobody here is lying to anybody on purpose. That's the worst part. They believe the chart because it's the only chart they've got. Then on Friday Hollis stood up at the all hands and said some people have been talking to Earth outside channels, and engineering information is released through the director's office. He didn't look at me. He didn't have to. So here's what I need. Don't share my logs. Not with the ARA, not with Quinn, not with the board, not with anybody. If Hollis goes looking for who's talking, he finds Bay D. Bay D isn't on his roster. If he finds it he shuts it, because rules, and it's the only thing up here making more air than last month. I'm not asking you to lie for me. I'm asking you not to hand me over. 729. Same minus nine. I'm so tired of writing minus nine, Dad. Love you. Ada out.

He watched it twice. The second time he stopped it on her face where she said hand me over, because he'd never heard her use those words about anything, and he wasn't sure she'd known she was going to.
At 6:30 Hollis Bayne's Monday report posted to the ARA's site, the way it did every Monday.

ARES STATION DIRECTOR'S WEEKLY REPORT TO THE ARA MONDAY, AUGUST 29, 2061 (EXTRACT). OXYGEN PLANT OPERATING WITHIN PROJECTED DEGRADATION. MARGIN: 796 DAYS (ARA MODEL). FAMILIES' BRIEFING OF AUGUST 25 RECEIVED WITH APPRECIATION. MORALE STRONG. PERSONNEL REMINDED THAT ENGINEERING INFORMATION IS RELEASED TO EARTH THROUGH THE DIRECTOR'S OFFICE.

Seven hundred and ninety six, and seven hundred and twenty nine. He had two numbers for the same thing, an official one and a private one, and the private one belonged to his daughter. He'd been the kind of crew chief who wrote up the gauge, not the pilot's opinion of it, and he knew which of the two numbers he'd have written up.

There was one more thing he knew, and it had taken him until 6:40 to remember it. The plant's cell voltages came down from Ares Station every sol in the engineering telemetry, to a server in the ARA's Denver office that nobody on the program read. It was the same data Ada used. It didn't have her name on it.

He writes to the board's clerk at 7:15. The first line says his daughter is on Ares Station and that the board should weigh what follows with that in mind. Then: the program has reason to believe the station's oxygen margin, as reported, may be overstated; he isn't the right person to judge it; the plant's cell voltage telemetry is on the ARA's Denver server; he asks the board to request an independent margin analysis from it, and to say so in its minutes, so the families' page isn't the only number anyone sees. He attaches nothing of hers. Then he records a log to Ada and tells her exactly what he did, the same day, as she asked him once to do with the bad things. The clerk's acknowledgment comes on Wednesday in the board's capitals: ARA MISSION ASSURANCE TO PROVIDE AN INDEPENDENT MARGIN ANALYSIS FROM STATION TELEMETRY FOR THE BOARD'S OCTOBER SESSION. RAPPORTEUR: R. CALDER.

Protect the person. Don't hide the fact. Her words stay hers, the safety question goes to governance through data the agency already holds, and the conflict goes in the first line. Then tell her what you did. Keep a confidence, put safety first, and disclose your own stake: three parts of the Code working together.
Tuesday, August 30. Frances Odum, who chaired Families of Ares, called his cell at 7:50 AM. She didn't say hello. She never had.

Malik sent me a message last night. He said, Mom, stop telling me fifty eight. He said some people up there think it's less. He wouldn't say who. A breath. I stood up at Thursday's briefing and thanked the agency for that chart. Families of Ares is putting out a statement on Friday. Simon Greaves wants a comment from me by Thursday. So I'm asking you, Mr. Okafor, because you're the one who answers. Was Thursday true?
He'd asked the board for an independent check of the margin the day before.
He thought about what Frances knew, and what Malik knew, and what he knew and couldn't say, and how close together those three things were on a station of two hundred and twelve people.

I can't tell you Thursday's number is right, ma'am. I can't tell you it's wrong. I can tell you it's in question, that people are being asked to check it against the plant's own data, and that I'll call you the day there's an answer. There's a long quiet on the line. That isn't reassuring, Frances says. No, ma'am. I believe it, though. Before he hangs up he asks one more thing: whether the families' statement could say what they don't know, along with what they were told. Friday's statement does. Then he calls Hale's office and tells Gwen Talley, her chief of staff, that the families' chair asked him, and what he said, so the Director hears it from him first.

Engaging a stakeholder means telling her what you know, what you don't, what's being done, and when she'll hear more, in words she can use with two hundred families. You don't expose your source and you don't vouch for a figure you doubt. Then you tell the sponsor.
Wednesday, September 7. 3:00 AM in Aurora, and Sam was awake because Quinn had texted him at 2:51, which she never did. One way light time twelve minutes and twenty two seconds.

ARES STATION ENGINEERING MORNING PACKET FROM C. OKONKWO. Third time this week someone at Watkins has pinged a station engineer's bunk between 2200 and 0600 our time. Monday it was about a log file's timestamp format. Last night it was a question about a font. Both marked urgent. My people are running a plant on six hours of sleep a sol, and now on less. Understood as: Earth's day has walked into our night again, and Earth thinks that's our problem. Three questions. What counts as urgent? Who on Earth is awake for us? And is the rest window a rule or a wish?
It was in the agreement, the line about ten at night to six in the morning. Seventeen names were under it.

Quinn had already found out who. Two of Rafa's engineers, both good, both twenty eight, both working at nine at night Watkins time because that was when the sim bay was free, and both honestly convinced that a question was urgent if the sprint review was Friday. The station's clock ran thirty nine and a half minutes later every sol. For half of every five weeks, Watkins's evening landed in the middle of the station's night.

He calls the two engineers in first, separately, and asks what happened, and they tell him: the sim bay, the Friday review, and nobody on Earth whose job it was to be awake for Mars. Then the team rewrites the line in the next packet, together. Urgent means someone could get hurt or the plant could be damaged. Everything else goes in the morning packet. Two Watkins engineers each week work Mars hours, paid as a shift, so there's always someone awake when the station is, and the inconvenience goes to Earth, which has more people. The engineer who asked about the font volunteers for the first week. Chiamaka's next packet ends with a line Quinn prints out and tapes over her desk. Understood as: a rule.

A broken ground rule is often a rule that doesn't fit the work. Find out why it broke, privately, then fix the rule with everyone it binds: define the terms, protect the people with less power, and share the cost of the time difference fairly.

Monday, September 12. Garrett's all hands was Thursday, in the high bay, on the pallet jack. Garrett's assistant had sent Sam the run of show. Item four: Tallgrass Courage Award, presented to Arlo Dunn, Stand 2, for his actions on the night of April 18. There was a plaque. Sam had seen it. It had a pronghorn on it.
Arlo's hands had healed in a week. On the night of April 18 he'd come in on the handline counting stanchions, and he'd said, since, that it was the most frightened he'd ever been.

Arlo came to Sam's office at seven, before his night shift on the stand, still in the knit cap with the ear flaps. I don't want it. He looked at the floor. I went out on the pad alone at night in a blizzard. The rule says don't. If I get a plaque for that, the next guy goes out too. He thought about it. And it wasn't me. It was everybody else getting me in.
Garrett, on the phone at eight, didn't see the problem. People need heroes, Sam. It's good for the floor.

He goes out to the stand at noon and asks them. They want three things, and none of them is a plaque. Their names on the near miss report as the people who fixed what failed. The roster rule read out loud at the all hands, so the habitat team hears it. And the coffee maker in the blockhouse replaced, because it's leaked since 2058. On Thursday Garrett stands on the pallet jack and reads the crew's names and the rule, and says the stand stopped a test in a blizzard to get a man in, and that he'd like every team in the building to be that boring. The new coffee maker arrives Friday. Arlo looks at it for a while. That's better than a plaque. You can't drink a plaque.

Recognize the team for the behaviors you want repeated, and ask the people being recognized how they'd like it. Public recognition of the right things spreads them. Represent the team's voice upward, even to the CEO's run of show.

Monday, September 19. Garrett's program status meeting ran ninety minutes on Monday mornings, in the boardroom with the view of the wind sock. Fourteen leads, one slide each, a color in the corner. The station engineers couldn't attend; it was the middle of their night, and since September 7 nobody was allowed to wake them for it.

Quinn had kept a tally, because she kept tallies. Twelve weeks. One hundred and sixty eight slides. Three yellows, no reds. In the same twelve weeks the issues log had gone from twenty two open items to forty one.

She'd found the reason the yellows stopped. In June the habitat thermal lead had shown yellow for a heater qualification. Garrett had laughed and said yellow was a color for people without a plan, and everybody had laughed, including her. The next Monday her slide was green. The heater qualification hadn't changed.

The notice under Rule 4.2 had gone to the partners by July 30, with Sam's name on it. On August 24 the partners had funded the year's next tranche and said they'd take up anything above the baseline against the October quarterly estimate. Bad news had gone out of this building on time once this summer. It hadn't come into this room in twelve weeks.

He asks six leads one question each, alone: what happens here when you bring bad news? The answers are short. You get a joke, one says, and then you get green. He takes the answers to Garrett with no names on them. Garrett laughs, and then reads them again, and doesn't. The next Monday Garrett opens the meeting standing at the head of the table. In June I made a joke about yellow. That was the most expensive joke I've told this year. I'd like the yellows back. The format changes the same day: written status in the log by Friday, so the station can read it and add theirs; Monday is thirty minutes on the three worst items, and the first person to bring a red gets thanked out loud. By the end of the month there are six yellows and one red. The red is the habitat heater, found in time.

Assess the culture before you change it: ask the people living in it what happens to bad news, privately, then work with the leader whose behavior set the norm. Redesign the meeting so it serves the whole team, including the members who can't attend live.

Friday, September 23. The board's clerk had written to the program on Wednesday. The Independent Readiness Board would hold a technical session on the Breather's control code on Wednesday, September 28, and requested that the person who ran the joint bench campaign present its results.
That was Quinn. She'd run the decision log, written half the hold rules, and answered every one of Chiamaka's three questions for six weeks, most of them before 6 AM.

She came to Sam's office at five, with the clerk's letter and her tablet against her chest, and closed the door behind her. You should do it. You're the program manager. I'm the scheduler. They'll ask things I can't answer, and it'll look like the program sent a kid. She put both hands flat on his desk. Bea used to do these.

She was twenty six. Two years older than Ada. He noticed it, the way he always did, and he noticed himself noticing, and for once he made himself look at what was actually in front of him: the person who knew more about the joint bench campaign than anyone on Earth, asking to be let off.

You're not a kid. You're the one who knows. I'll be in the room, and I won't talk unless you look at me. They rehearse Saturday and Monday, at the big room table, with Sam asking the worst questions he can think of. On Tuesday he sends her out to Byers to see someone who answered that board's questions for three hours in May. Wendell gives her coffee from the thermos and one piece of advice. Answer the question they asked. Then stop. On Wednesday she presents for forty minutes. The board asks about hold rule nineteen, and she answers it and stops. Sam doesn't speak once. On the way to the truck she says, Ruth wrote something down when I stopped. She does that.

Mentoring is part of leading a team. When someone on your team is asked to do something hard and visible, coach them, rehearse with them, let them own it, and connect them with a mentor who's done it. Then stay out of the way.

Monday, September 26. Page six came in the mail. HOSE WASHER was still on the list on the refrigerator, under page five, and the washer from Kiowa Creek was still in its bag by the sink. Green ink, Golden postmark. He read it at the kitchen table with the butter knife beside it.
1100 MOVED TATE AFT IN THE SIM AND TO THE OTHER END OF THE CREW TABLE. MORI FORWARD. FIXED.
Tate and Mori were two of the Petrel's crew. Earlier on the same page they'd stopped speaking to each other over who got to make the abort call.

He read the 1100 line four times. Then he thought about the upper deck of the stand, behind the oxidizer tank, and Hana saying including Mars, and Rafa on the recording a week later, apologizing to the same seventeen people. He hadn't moved anybody's chair. He'd been tempted to.
And the 1600 line, which he read last and longest. DOES THE CREW KNOW ABOUT CYCLE 3. TOLD HIM THE CREW HAS ENOUGH TO THINK ABOUT.

Ada's answer to the log where he'd told her about the board had come on September 2. You didn't send them me. You sent them the plant. I didn't know you could do that. Okay. That's allowed. Then, after a pause he'd watched twice, Tell me when they say a number. The same day.

Thursday, September 29. 4:10 PM. The simulator bay at Watkins had its lights down, the way Rafa liked it for a run that mattered, and twenty people stood around the edges of the room with their arms folded, which was how engineers watched things they cared about. Commander Yusra Haddad stood at the back. Hana stood by the door with her deputy.

Build A1. The first autonomy build: the departure burn, uncrewed, from ignition to cutoff, with nobody's hands on anything. The valve in its model had the rebound in it, cycle three after a cold soak, because Hana's rule said it had to.

Run one. The burn lit on time. The simulated stage pushed against the simulated Earth for nineteen minutes, and the guidance trimmed it the way a person would have, a little late and then exactly right, and at cutoff the main oxidizer valve closed and stayed closed, and the trajectory on the big screen bent away toward a dot labeled MARS 2063. Somebody at the back said yes, quietly, and then everybody did, louder.

Run two failed at four minutes, a timing race in the guidance loop. Run three held on a sensor that wasn't broken. Runs four through nine failed in five different ways, and two of them were ways nobody had a name for yet. At 7:40 Rafa turned the lights up.
Once is a fact, he said. Twice is a capability. We've got a fact. He didn't sound disappointed. He sounded like a man who'd been told what his next three months were.

Driving home, Sam went back over the ten weeks. Seventeen people on two planets had argued, and mostly not on the loop. Bea was cutting keys. Ada's peppers had come up. He let himself have that much, the whole way home.

At eight thirty he sat down at the kitchen table and pressed record. One way light time thirteen minutes and twenty one seconds. Next June it would be just over twenty one, and in a month the question and its answer would take close to half an hour, and none of it was going to hurry for him. He told her about the sim bay, and the lights, and the dot on the screen, and that it had worked once.

He told her about Quinn at the board, too, and Wendell's coffee, and the answer she'd given and then stopped. She's two years older than you, he said. I keep noticing. I'm trying to notice her instead.

He didn't tell her about Kiowa Creek Hardware, or the key machine, or four pages in square capitals at the board. That wasn't his. He told her he'd found Bea, and that she was all right, and that she cut keys now and was good at it.

The meeting that closed AR 2207 had taken twenty two minutes. He didn't tell her that. He wrote it in the notebook instead: TWENTY TWO MINUTES. The round trip to her, the week the bench opened. A question and its answer. He didn't do the voice. He sent it. It would be on Mars before he'd brushed his teeth.
Under SAME DAY, a few lines down, he wrote ONCE. Over the high bay doors, thirty five minutes east, the countdown clock had rolled over to 507.
